Languages of antiquity

Armenians and Georgians

The Caucasus · from Mashtots's alphabet to the three Georgian scripts

At a glance

Region
the Armenian Highlands (today's Armenia and eastern Turkey); in present-day Georgia, the kingdoms of Kartli (Iberia) and Colchis
Period
Armenian and Georgian kingdoms from the last centuries BCE; native scripts from the early 5th century CE
Languages
Armenian (an independent branch of Indo-European) and Georgian (Kartvelian family), unrelated to each other
Scripts
the Armenian alphabet (36, later 38 letters); the Georgian scripts Asomtavruli, Nuskhuri and Mkhedruli
Earliest evidence
Georgian inscriptions from Bir el Qutt near Bethlehem (conventionally dated c. 430) and Bolnisi (493/494); Armenian inscriptions from the later 5th century
Today
Armenian has more than 5 million speakers, Georgian about 4 million; Grabar and Old Georgian remain liturgical languages

At the start of the 5th century two Christian peoples of the South Caucasus acquired scripts of their own. The Armenian alphabet, devised by tradition around 405 by the monk Mesrop Mashtots, and the Georgian script, whose origin is still disputed, have been in continuous use for more than fifteen hundred years. The languages they write are unrelated: Armenian forms a branch of its own within the Indo-European family, while Georgian belongs to the small Kartvelian family, for which no relationship to any other language has been demonstrated.

Between Rome and Persia

Armenia lay on the Armenian Highlands between Asia Minor, Mesopotamia and the Caucasus, in lands once ruled by Urartu. From the early 2nd century BCE it was governed by a native dynasty, the Artaxiads, and later by a branch of the Parthian Arsacids. For centuries the country stood between two great powers, Rome and the Parthian, later the Sasanian, Empire. In 387 the two empires partitioned it; about four-fifths went to Persia, and the Armenian kingdom there was abolished in 428.

North of Armenia lay the Georgian kingdoms: in the east Kartli, which Greek and Roman writers called Iberia, with its capital at Mtskheta; in the west, on the Black Sea, Colchis. Both countries became Christian in the 4th century: Armenia by tradition in 301 under King Tiridates III (some scholars prefer a later date), Kartli under King Mirian III in 326 or 337. Before that, both wrote in foreign languages and scripts, mainly Aramaic and Greek: the bilingual Greek-Aramaic gravestone from Armazi near Mtskheta dates from the first centuries CE, and Armenian kings struck coins with Aramaic and Greek legends.

Two unrelated languages

Armenian forms a branch of its own within the Indo-European family, like Greek or Albanian. Its relationship to the other Indo-European languages is masked by sound changes: Armenian hayr “father” corresponds to Latin pater because initial p became h in Armenian. According to Gevorg Jahukyan, only about 1,500 words survive from Proto-Indo-European; many others were borrowed from Iranian languages, above all Parthian. For this reason Armenian was long taken for an Iranian language, until in 1875 Heinrich Hübschmann used the comparative method to separate the Iranian loans from the inherited vocabulary. A widely held hypothesis (Holger Pedersen, Antoine Meillet) sees Greek as its closest relative; the question remains open.

Georgian belongs to the Kartvelian family together with Mingrelian, Laz and Svan. No relationship to any other family, including the other Caucasian families, has been demonstrated. Georgian is agglutinative: a verb can mark both subject and object and may contain up to eight morphemes; the subject of a transitive verb in the past tense stands in the ergative case; there is no grammatical gender and no article; and numbers from 20 to 99 are counted in twenties. In Georgian mama means “father” and deda “mother”; the resemblance to nursery words elsewhere is coincidental.

Armenian words have counterparts in other Indo-European languages, though sound changes often disguise them. Georgian words of the same meaning are unrelated:

Mashtots and the Armenian alphabet

Armenian sources agree that the Armenian alphabet was created by Mesrop Mashtots (c. 361–440). The main source is his biography, written in the 440s by his pupil Koryun. Mashtots knew Greek, Persian and Syriac and served at the royal court in Vagharshapat before becoming a monk and preacher. At the time, Armenian churches read from Greek and Syriac books, and the text had to be interpreted.

With the support of Catholicos Sahak Part'ev and King Vramshapuh he set out to find a script for Armenian. According to Koryun he first tried letters kept by a Syrian bishop named Daniel (the so-called Danielian letters), but they proved inadequate. He then travelled to Edessa and Samosata in northern Mesopotamia; there he completed an alphabet of 36 letters, and a Greek scribe named Rufinus gave the letters their final form. By tradition it dates to 405; the Armenian linguist Hrachia Acharian arrived at 404.

Mashtots went on to found schools in which the young learned the new script, and sent pupils to Edessa, Constantinople, Alexandria and other centres of learning to obtain Greek manuscripts. The Bible was first translated from Syriac and then again from the Greek Septuagint; this version, completed around 434, is still used by the Armenian Church. Mashtots died in 440 and is buried at Oshakan. The Armenian Church venerates him as a saint and, together with others, celebrates the Feast of the Holy Translators.

Letters on a Greek model

The Armenian script is a true alphabet: unlike the Syriac or Pahlavi scripts, it has separate letters for all vowels, as Greek does. On the prevailing view Greek was also its model. The order of the letters broadly follows the Greek alphabet, with letters for sounds that Greek lacks (such as ž, x, c or č) inserted among them, and the shapes of some letters, such as թ, փ and բ, recall Greek θ, φ and β. Other scholars have also looked for models in the Pahlavi or Syriac scripts; exactly how Mashtots designed the letter shapes is unknown.

The letters also served as numerals, as in Greek: the first nine stand for units, the next nine for tens, then hundreds and thousands up to Ք = 9000. In the Middle Ages two letters were added, Օ for o and Ֆ for f, bringing the alphabet to 38 letters. The oldest hand is the erkatagir majuscule (“iron letters”); from the 10th century it gave rise to the rounder bolorgir, the basis of printed type from the 16th century, and to other cursive hands. Soviet Armenia reformed the spelling in the 1920s. Armenians abroad, most of whom speak Western Armenian, and Armenians in Iran continue to use the traditional orthography.

Grabar: the language of translators and scholars

The Armenian of the 5th century is called Grabar, “the literary language”; it is the earliest attested form of Armenian. Mashtots's pupils translated not only the Bible but also the liturgy, the decrees of the church councils and works of the Greek and Syriac Church Fathers. Some works survive only in Armenian: the first part of Eusebius's Chronicle (the Chronography), for instance, of which only fragments remain in Greek, is known complete only from the Armenian translation. An original literature, historiography and philosophy arose as well, and Armenian tradition regards the 5th century as a golden age.

Grabar remained the literary language until the 19th century; even the first Armenian periodical, Azdarar, published from 1794 in Madras in India, appeared in Grabar. Meanwhile spoken Armenian had changed, and in the 19th century two new literary standards emerged: Eastern Armenian, centred on Tbilisi and later Yerevan, and Western Armenian in Istanbul. Grabar remains the liturgical language of the Armenian Church, and for comparative linguistics it is an important witness in reconstructing Proto-Indo-European.

The Matenadaran

An exceptionally large number of Armenian manuscripts survive, although many were lost in wars: according to the medieval historian Stepanos Orbelian, the Seljuks burned more than 10,000 manuscripts at the fortress of Baghaberd in 1170. They were kept in the libraries of the great monasteries, such as Haghpat, Sanahin or Tatev. In Armenian such a library is called a matenadaran, “repository of books”; both parts of the word are of Middle Persian origin.

The largest collection today is held by the Matenadaran in Yerevan, the Mesrop Mashtots Institute of Ancient Manuscripts. Its core is the library of the Catholicosate at Etchmiadzin, nationalised in 1920; the institute was founded as such in 1959 and has borne Mashtots's name since 1962. It holds some 23,000 manuscripts and fragments, in Armenian and other languages, and since 1997 its collection has been on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register. The Vehamor Gospel, probably of the 7th century, is regarded as the oldest complete Armenian book; the Lazarian Gospel of 887 (named after the Lazarev Institute in Moscow) is also among the oldest volumes in the collection. The Etchmiadzin Gospels of 989 are bound in ivory covers of the 6th century.

The Etchmiadzin Gospels

The beginnings of Georgian writing

Georgian writing is attested from the 5th century. Most scholars link its creation to the Christianisation of Kartli, so it most likely arose between the conversion of King Mirian III and the earliest surviving inscriptions. From the outset it served for translating the Bible and church texts, made by monks both in Georgia and in Palestine. Fragmentary inscriptions from Nekresi in Kakheti, which Levan Chilashvili dated in the 1980s to the 2nd or 1st century BCE, have not been accepted as that old by other scholars.

The oldest surviving Georgian inscriptions come not from Georgia but from the Holy Land. In 1952 the Italian archaeologist Virgilio Canio Corbo excavated a Georgian monastery at Bir el Qutt, about 2 km north of Bethlehem, with a mosaic floor bearing four inscriptions in Asomtavruli. Two of them are conventionally dated to around 430; one, on the usual reading, names Peter the Iberian, a Georgian prince and later monk, still by his secular name Maruan. The dating rests on the people named in the inscriptions and is not entirely certain. The surviving inscriptions are kept at the Terra Sancta Museum (Studium Biblicum Franciscanum) in Jerusalem; the one bearing Maruan's name has been lost. In Georgia itself the oldest inscriptions are in Bolnisi Sioni Cathedral south-west of Tbilisi: according to one of them, building began in the 20th year of the Persian king Peroz and was completed 15 years later, that is, in 493/494.

Mashtots or Pharnavaz?

Who created the Georgian script is disputed. Mashtots's biographer Koryun states that Mashtots also devised scripts for the Georgians and the Caucasian Albanians. This account was taken up by medieval Armenian sources and is accepted by some modern scholars; Hrachia Acharian defended it and dated the Georgian script to 408. Georgian scholarship and some Western scholars reject it: the historian Ivane Javakhishvili considered the passage a later interpolation of the 6th–7th century, and the linguist Tamaz Gamkrelidze objected that creating a script would have required a thorough analysis of the language, whereas Mashtots did not know Georgian. Others allow that Armenian clerics took part in its creation, not necessarily Mashtots himself; Ghazar Parpetsi (5th century) credits Mashtots with the Armenian script only.

The Georgian chronicle The Lives of the Kings of Kartli (c. 800) credits the script to a far earlier king, Pharnavaz, of the 3rd century BCE. Scholars regard this as legend, since there is no archaeological evidence for it. According to more recent work, the Georgian alphabet preserves the order and numerical values of the Greek letters more faithfully than the Armenian one does. This closeness to the Greek alphabet is cited among the arguments that the Georgian script was not modelled on the Armenian.

Three scripts, one alphabet

Over its history Georgian has been written in three scripts, which share the same letter names and the same order and are written from left to right. The oldest is Asomtavruli (“capital letters”, also Mrgvlovani, “rounded”), from the 5th century: letters of equal height made of curves and right angles. In the 9th century it developed into the slanted, more angular Nuskhuri; the oldest inscription in this script, from 835, is in the church of Ateni Sioni, and the oldest manuscripts date from 864. Church manuscripts written in Nuskhuri with Asomtavruli capitals in titles and at the start of paragraphs are called Khutsuri, “clerical script”.

The third script, Mkhedruli (“of horsemen, military”), appears in the 10th century; its oldest inscription, from 982, is also at Ateni Sioni. At first it served secular purposes, for example in the royal charters of Bagrat IV in the 11th century, and in the 19th century, with printing, it became the only script in everyday use for Georgian. The alphabet originally had 38 letters; the Society for the Spreading of Literacy among Georgians, founded in 1879 by Ilia Chavchavadze, dropped five redundant ones, leaving the 33 in use today. Mkhedruli has no distinction of upper and lower case; the capital forms called Mtavruli are used only in all-capitals text and were added to Unicode in 2018. In 2016 UNESCO inscribed the living culture of the three Georgian scripts on its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

The order and numerical values of the letters match the Greek alphabet: vin, in sixth place, has the value 6, like Greek digamma; he, in eighth place, corresponds to Greek eta; and hie, with the value 60, to Greek xi. Letters for sounds that Greek lacks, such as š, č, c, x or ǯ, stand mostly at the end. Asomtavruli wrote the sound u with the pair ႭჃ (o + w), like Greek ου; in Nuskhuri the pair became a single letter.

Old Georgian

The language of the earliest texts is called Old Georgian (5th–11th centuries). In its earliest layer (5th–8th centuries) two varieties are distinguished, Khanmeti and Haemeti, named after a verbal prefix kh- or h- where later Classical Old Georgian has h-, s- or nothing. From this period only about a dozen inscriptions and eight manuscripts with religious texts survive, often palimpsests, that is, parchments whose original text was scraped off and written over. The oldest literary work is the Martyrdom of the Holy Queen Shushanik, attributed to Iakob Tsurtaveli in the 5th century.

From the start, Georgian monks were active abroad as well: in Palestine, in St Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai and, from the 10th century, on Mount Athos, where the Georgian monastery of Iviron was founded. Old Georgian remained the language of the Georgian Orthodox Church, and modern Georgians can largely understand it. In the 11th–12th centuries it gave way to Middle Georgian, whose most famous work is Shota Rustaveli's epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin, of the 12th century. The first books printed (partly) in Georgian appeared in 1629.

The third script of the Caucasus

Koryun also credits Mashtots with a script for the Caucasian Albanians, a people living in what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan, who spoke a Northeast Caucasian language. The script was in use from the 5th to the 12th century and was then forgotten. Only in 1937 did the Georgian scholar Ilia Abuladze find its alphabet in a 15th-century Armenian manuscript in the Matenadaran (No. 7117) that compares several alphabets. Short inscriptions from excavations at Mingachevir followed in 1947–1952.

Connected texts were found only in St Catherine's Monastery on Mount Sinai: in 1996 the Georgian scholar Zaza Aleksidze recognised, beneath the Georgian text of some palimpsests, a lower layer written in the Albanian script (announced in 1997). It contains fragments of a lectionary and of the Gospel of John, published in 2008 by Aleksidze, Jost Gippert and others; only thanks to them can the language now largely be read. The alphabet has 52 letters, and according to Gippert its structure depends on the Armenian alphabet much as the Armenian depends on the Greek. Udi, spoken by some 8,000 people, is considered the last descendant of Caucasian Albanian.
